label: explain2-bm-science
one_line: We test whether printed two-layer plastic strips can curl with damp air, using a maths limit that a computer has checked.
what:
A pine cone scale is two layers stuck together. When the air dries, one layer shrinks more than the other. The scale bends open. We ask if a 3D printer can make strips that do the same with ordinary printing plastic.

Here is a plain example. Take a strip 40 millimetres long and 0.8 millimetres thick. That is about as long as your thumb and eight hairs thick. Say one layer grows 0.1 to 0.3 percent more than the other when it soaks up water. That is our own estimate, not a measurement. The best possible bend is then a circle about 20 to 60 centimetres wide. The tip of the strip moves only about 1 to 4 millimetres.

Where does "best possible" come from? An engineer named Timoshenko published a bending formula in 1925. A computer program that accepts only complete proofs has confirmed one limit in it. The limit says a strip can never curl tighter than 1.5 times the mismatch, divided by its thickness. The mismatch is how much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length. A mismatch of 0.2 percent is written 0.002. We use the limit to rule out hopeless designs on paper before we print anything.
why:
Plants move with no motor and no power. A printed part that did this could be useful. Printing a strip and then waiting days to see nothing happen wastes time. A rule that rules out hopeless designs saves that time.

The limit is not new. A 2015 paper by Holstov had already drawn it on a graph. What is new is that a computer has now proved it. We do not know yet if a real printed strip will follow the formula. We have not printed one.

Real pine cones show what is possible. A cone scale 1 millimetre thick bends about 1.3 per centimetre between dry and soaked air. That is a circle about 8 millimetres wide. Printing plastic swells far less than a cone does, so our strips would bend much more gently.

wrong_if: Here is the bet, written before we looked. We say a printed two-layer strip will never curl tighter than 1.5 times the mismatch divided by its thickness. If we measure a real strip that curls tighter, we are wrong. We also bet that thin layers react faster, by roughly the square of the thickness. So a layer half as thick should be about four times quicker. If it is not much faster, we are wrong about that part. And if a stiff printed layer on a soft one curls far less than the formula says, the formula is not useful here.
could_go_wrong: The formula is for a thin ribbon. A wide sheet behaves differently. It can curl about 30 to 50 percent tighter, but only in one direction.
Water soaks into printed plastic very slowly. A demonstration could take days instead of minutes.
The formula says nothing about speed. It also ignores creep, which is slow sagging under a steady push. It does not cover how well the two layers stay glued.
Printing plastics may swell too little to give a bend you can see.
Two documents from Formlabs, a company that makes 3D printers, disagree on how much one resin swells in water. They probably describe two versions of it.
Heat may bend a strip more than damp air does. That would confuse the test unless we vary both.
We could not read three of the original papers in full. Some of what we say about them is second-hand.

questions.q: What is the mismatch, and how is it measured?
questions.a: It is how much more one layer lengthens than the other, as a fraction of its length. If one layer grows 1 millimetre per metre more, the mismatch is 0.001, or 0.1 percent. No one has measured it for printed strips in damp air. Our numbers are estimates.

questions.q: What would a real strip look like?
questions.a: Our example is 40 millimetres long and 0.8 millimetres thick, with a mismatch of 0.1 to 0.3 percent. The tightest possible bend is a circle about 20 to 60 centimetres wide. The tip would move about 1 to 4 millimetres. A real strip would bend less than this. Nobody has printed or measured one yet.

questions.q: How do you know the limit is true?
questions.a: A proof-checking program accepted it, using only the three standard starting rules of maths. It also rejected a false version that said 7/5 instead of 3/2. A 2015 paper had also shown the same limit on a graph.

We have not printed or measured any strip. We could not read some original papers in full. We did not test wide sheets, big swelling, creep or glue between layers. The speed numbers for plastics are our own estimates.
No. The limit was already known from graphs. The new part is that a computer has proved it.

questions.q: Do real pine cones reach the limit?
questions.a: Close, but not quite. By our own arithmetic they reach about 82 to 97 percent of it.

questions.q: Why not use a stiffer partner layer to curl more?
questions.a: Because the best bend needs balance. A stiffer layer must be made thinner to balance a softer one. When the two are balanced, the stiffness difference no longer changes the result. Only the mismatch and the total thickness set the limit. So a stiffer partner cannot beat it.

questions.q: Does ordinary printing plastic swell much in water?
questions.a: Mostly little. A one-centimetre cube of two Formlabs resins gains about 0.7 percent in weight in a day. That is about a sixth of a drop of water for a cube weighing 1.2 grams. One other resin sheet gained 8 percent in a day. So it depends on the resin and the test.

questions.q: How fast could a printed strip move?
questions.a: Our model says a layer 0.2 to 0.4 millimetres thick of a stiff stock resin takes about 9 to 38 hours to soak. A layer 0.8 millimetres or thicker could take days. These are model results, not measurements. We do not know of any measured soaking speed for these resins.

questions.q: Does the formula match what others measured?
questions.a: It follows the trends. But it predicts a bend about four times tighter than printed soft humidity strips actually made. So the formula gives the best case, not the typical case.

glossary.plain: A thin strip made of two materials stuck face to face.
How much more one layer swells or shrinks than the other, as a fraction of its length.
How tightly a strip bends. A tighter bend means a smaller circle.
A number for how sharp a bend is. It is one divided by the width of the circle the strip follows.
A value the answer can never go above.
Software that accepts a maths argument only if every step is complete.
The name of the proof-checking program we used.
A rule written in maths that turns inputs into an answer.
How hard a material pushes back when you try to bend or stretch it.
How many times stiffer one layer is than the other.
Grow a little in size as water soaks in.
The liquid plastic that some 3D printers harden with light.
A company that makes resin 3D printers.
Slow change in shape under a steady push.
A calculation that imitates how something should behave.

glossary.plain: A program that splits a strip into tiny pieces and works out how each one moves.
Parts in every hundred.
One thousandth of a metre. A hair is about 0.1 millimetre thick.
A material that changes shape when the air gets more or less damp, like a pine cone scale.
How much water vapour is in the air.
The engineer who published the bending formula in 1925.
The author of a 2015 paper that had already drawn the limit on a graph.
A complete argument that leaves no gap.
A plate much wider than it is thick. It bends differently from a narrow ribbon.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the proof checks. Three should pass, and one deliberately bad proof should fail.
check_yourself.expect: Three files say ALL CHECKED with no errors. The deliberately bad proof says FAILED. That failure is the right result.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the bending arithmetic. It checks the limit, the 1925 formula match, and the soaking times.
check_yourself.expect: The top value over a grid of test cases is 1.5, to 15 decimal places. A soaking-time constant of 0.7239 also appears.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the plain arithmetic for the pine cone, the water uptake in drops, and the thin-layer speed-up.
check_yourself.expect: 0.7 percent turns into 7 milligrams per gram. The soaking constant 0.848 appears.
A top value of 1.5 on the test grid, and 1.25 for the pine cone in Reyssat and Mahadevan.

check_yourself.what: Open the pine cone paper and read how the two layers work.
check_yourself.expect: A paper titled Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers.
